title: Problem Overview and Imports
content: **Problem Overview.** Erdős Problem #679 asks: are there infinitely many n such that ω(n-k) < (1+ε) log k / log log k for all sufficiently large k < n? The main question is OPEN. The stronger version with O(1) error is FALSE. Imports Mathlib arithmetic function infrastructure and real analysis.
mathContext: The problem asks whether infinitely many integers n have the property that all their 'predecessors' n-k (for large k) have unusually few prime factors. By the Hardy-Ramanujan theorem, the normal order of ω(m) is log log m, which for m = n-k ≈ k means ω(n-k) ≈ log log k. The threshold (1+ε) log k / log log k is much larger than log log k, so the question asks if all predecessors can simultaneously avoid being 'prime-factor rich' — having many more distinct prime factors than typical. The (1+ε) multiplicative slack distinguishes this from the disproven O(1) version.

title: The ω Function and Properties
content: **omega.** ω(n) = |{p prime : p | n}|, the number of distinct prime divisors of n. Basic properties: ω(1) = 0, ω(p) = 1 for primes, ω(p^k) = 1 for prime powers, and ω is completely additive on coprime arguments: ω(mn) = ω(m) + ω(n) when gcd(m,n) = 1.
mathContext: The function ω is the prototypical **additive arithmetic function**: it satisfies ω(mn) = ω(m) + ω(n) for coprime m, n. This additivity is the foundation of the Erdős-Kac theorem, which shows that (ω(n) - log log n)/√(log log n) converges in distribution to the standard normal — making ω behave like a sum of independent random variables. The Lean definition uses `Nat.primeFactors.card`, which counts the distinct elements of the multiset of prime factors.

title: Hardy-Ramanujan Normal Order
content: **Hardy-Ramanujan (1917).** The normal order of ω(n) is log log n: for almost all n (density 1), ω(n) is within a (1±ε) factor of log log n. Also: the maximum of ω(n) for n ≤ x is approximately log x / log log x.
mathContext: The Hardy-Ramanujan theorem (1917) is one of the landmark results of analytic number theory. It says that 'typical' integers have about log log n distinct prime factors — a doubly logarithmic function that grows extremely slowly (log log 10^{100} ≈ 5.4). The proof uses the first and second moments of ω(n) computed via the prime harmonic sum. The maximum value of ω for n ≤ x is much larger: ~ log x / log log x, achieved by primorials p₁p₂...pᵣ. This gap between normal and extremal behavior is central to Problem #679, which asks whether n-k can simultaneously avoid the extremal regime for all k.

title: Threshold Function and Main Conjecture
content: **threshold and MainConjecture.** The threshold function is (1+ε) log k / log log k — the maximum possible ω value times a (1+ε) factor. The property requires ω(n-k) < threshold(ε, k) for all large k < n. The main conjecture asks: are there infinitely many such n? The answer is OPEN.
mathContext: The threshold (1+ε) log k / log log k equals (1+ε) times the maximal order of ω for integers near k. Thus the question asks: can all predecessors n-k simultaneously have ω below (1+ε) times the maximum? Since ω(m) < log m / log log m for 'almost all' m (Hardy-Ramanujan), the condition is satisfied by each individual k with high probability. The difficulty is the **simultaneous** requirement: as k ranges over all large values below n, the events 'ω(n-k) < threshold' must all hold. These events are not independent due to the arithmetic structure of n-k values, making the problem extremely hard.

title: Stronger Version (Disproven)
content: **StrongerVersion is FALSE.** The version with O(1) error — asking whether ω(n-k) < log k / log log k + C for a constant C — is disproven. In fact, for all large n, there exists k < n with ω(n-k) ≥ log k / log log k + c · log k / (log log k)², where c > 0 is an absolute constant.
mathContext: The disproof shows that the (1+ε) multiplicative slack is essential: without it, even a bounded additive correction fails. The quantitative lower bound ω(n-k) ≥ log k/log log k + c · log k/(log log k)² means that for every large n, some predecessor n-k exceeds the threshold by a secondary term of order log k/(log log k)². This is proven by a counting argument: among the residues n-k for k near e^{e^j}, sufficiently many must have ω above the sharp threshold. The gap between the O(1) (false) and (1+ε) (open) versions highlights the delicate nature of the problem.

title: Ω Function Variant
content: **bigOmega and OmegaVariant.** Ω(n) counts prime factors with multiplicity (so Ω(12) = Ω(2²·3) = 3, while ω(12) = 2). Since Ω(n) ≥ ω(n) always, the appropriate threshold for the Ω variant is log₂ k = log k / log 2, which is the maximum of Ω for n ≤ k (achieved by powers of 2).
mathContext: The function Ω is **completely additive**: Ω(mn) = Ω(m) + Ω(n) for all m, n (not just coprime). Its maximum for n ≤ k is log₂ k (achieved by 2^{⌊log₂ k⌋}), compared to ω's maximum of ~ log k / log log k. The Ω variant asks the same question but with the Ω-appropriate threshold. Since Ω(n) = ω(n) for squarefree n and most integers are 'nearly squarefree,' the two variants are closely related but the Ω version has a different threshold scale.

title: Special Cases: Powers of 2 and Primorials
content: **Special n values.** For n = 2^m (power of 2): there exists k < 2^m with ω(2^m - k) ≥ log k / log log k. For n = primorial(r) = p₁·p₂·...·pᵣ: ω(primorial(r)) = r, so primorials are prime-factor-rich. The primorial definition uses `Nat.nth Nat.Prime` to select the r-th prime.
mathContext: Powers of 2 and primorials represent extremes of the prime factorization spectrum: 2^m has ω = 1 (one distinct prime factor) but Ω = m, while primorial(r) has ω = r (all distinct) and Ω = r (squarefree). Testing n = 2^m is natural because 2^m - k ranges over all odd numbers below 2^m, and some of these must have many prime factors by a counting argument. Primorials are the 'greedily prime-rich' numbers, analogous to highly composite numbers for the τ function. The property SatisfiesProperty(ε, n) is hardest to achieve for n with structured factorization.

title: Lower Bounds on ω(n-k)
content: **existence_of_large_omega.** For any n ≥ 10, there exists k with 2 ≤ k < n and ω(n-k) ≥ (log log n)/2. Also: the set of k with ω(n-k) ≤ 2 has density strictly less than 1 in {0,...,n-1}.
mathContext: These lower bounds show that some predecessor n-k must have a reasonable number of prime factors. The bound ω(n-k) ≥ (log log n)/2 follows from the Hardy-Ramanujan theorem applied to the residues n-1, n-2, ..., 1: since ω(m) ≥ (log log m)/2 for 'most' m, at least one of the n-1 values n-k must satisfy this. The density bound on {k : ω(n-k) ≤ 2} uses the fact that integers with at most 2 prime factors (semiprimes and below) have density approaching 0 in a precise sense.

title: Connections to Problems #248 and #413
content: **Related problems.** Problem #248 (bounded prime factors of consecutive integers) asks about ω(n+k) growth; solved affirmatively by Tao-Teräväinen. Problem #413 (barriers for the omega function) studies the barrier property m + ω(m) ≤ n. Both are placeholder connections in the current formalization.
mathContext: Problem #248 asks whether infinitely many n exist with ω(n+k) growing at most linearly in k — a 'forward' version of #679's 'backward' question about n-k. The Tao-Teräväinen solution to #248 uses deep sieve-theoretic methods. Problem #413 studies 'ω-barriers': integers n such that m + ω(m) ≤ n for all m < n. These barriers encode structural constraints on the ω function that connect to #679's simultaneous small-ω requirement. The placeholder definitions `Problem248Connection` and `Problem413Connection` indicate these relationships without formalizing the precise links.

title: Probabilistic Heuristics
content: **Heuristics and expected count.** Probabilistic reasoning suggests random n should NOT satisfy the property: among the many predecessors n-k, at least one is expected to have ω exceeding the threshold. The expected count of special n ≤ x is heuristically ~ x / log x.
mathContext: The probabilistic heuristic treats the values ω(n-1), ω(n-2), ..., ω(1) as 'approximately independent' random variables, each with the Hardy-Ramanujan distribution. The probability that a single m has ω(m) ≥ (1+ε) log m / log log m is about 1/(log m)^{ε + o(1)} by large deviation estimates for additive functions. With ~ n such values, the expected number exceeding the threshold is ~ n / (log n)^ε, which grows with n. This suggests the simultaneous condition fails for most n, but the heuristic x/log x count of survivors is positive — neither confirming nor denying the conjecture. The non-independence of the ω(n-k) values (arising from shared prime factors) is the fundamental obstacle.

title: Key Dichotomy
content: **dichotomy.** Either the MainConjecture holds (infinitely many special n exist) or there is a uniform lower bound: for all large n, some k < n has ω(n-k) ≥ (1+c) log k / log log k with c > 0. This is an excluded-middle formalization of the problem's two possible outcomes.
mathContext: The dichotomy cleanly separates the two possible worlds. If the conjecture fails, the negation gives: for all ε > 0, only finitely many n satisfy the property. Compactness arguments then yield a uniform c > 0 such that for all large n, some predecessor n-k has ω 'overshooting' by a multiplicative (1+c) factor. This dichotomy is useful because different proof strategies apply in each case: the positive case requires constructing infinitely many special n, while the negative case requires exhibiting large-ω predecessors universally.

title: Density Considerations
content: **Density bounds.** If special n exist, they are sparse: the count of n ≤ x satisfying the property is at most x / log x. The DensityQuestion asks whether the count is even sparser — at most x^α for some α < 1.
mathContext: The density bound #{n ≤ x : SatisfiesProperty(ε, n)} ≤ x / log x shows that even if infinitely many special n exist, they form a zero-density subset of the integers (since x/log x = o(x)). The proof uses the fact that for each special n, all predecessors n-k must avoid the set of prime-factor-rich integers, which constrains n to avoid many residue classes. The question whether the count is actually x^α for α < 1 (polynomial but sublinear) would indicate these n are much rarer than primes.
